claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys inherently possess atomic-level chemical homogeneity.
High configurational entropy drives atomic-level homogeneity in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Atomic-level homogeneity kinetically mitigates vacancy-assisted diffusion during high-temperature vacuum annealing.
Atomic-level homogeneity mitigates elemental segregation during high-temperature vacuum annealing.
Mitigation of vacancy-assisted diffusion and segregation stabilizes both the structure and chemical composition of high-entropy nanoalloys.
The proposed initial high-entropy nanoalloys have a uniform, random distribution of constituent elements.
High-temperature annealing induces dynamic atomic reordering that acts as a self-healing process.
Dynamic atomic reordering counters vacancy-induced clustering and segregation.
High configurational entropy favors continuous and reversible rearrangement of constituent atoms during annealing.
Continuous reversible atomic rearrangement suppresses segregated-cluster formation by re-establishing a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Thermal annealing activates vacancy formation and associated diffusion processes.
Under comparable annealing conditions, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less elemental segregation than low-entropy counterparts.
High-entropy nanoalloys will maintain nanoscale elemental uniformity during annealing.
Incipient segregation appearing at intermediate annealing stages will reverse with continued annealing.
Surface diffusion is activated in the approximate temperature range of 600–900 °C.
The prediction is limited to annealing at approximately 600–900 °C under high-vacuum conditions.
At temperatures beyond the stated range, additional phase transformations may dominate behavior.
In non-vacuum environments, oxidation or other environmental effects may dominate behavior.
